stem: A colleague says effective compute has grown mainly because data centers now hold far more GPUs than before. What does this overlook about how effective compute is defined?

options.text: Effective compute multiplies chip count by hardware efficiency by software efficiency, and each factor can rise independently of the other two.
Effective compute is essentially chip count restated in different units, so tracking chip totals alone already explains most of the trend.
options.provenance: misreads 'compute means more than just counting GPUs' as a minor caveat rather than the section's central redefinition of the term

options.text: Effective compute rises only when chip count, hardware efficiency, and software efficiency increase at the same time.
options.provenance: misreads the multiplication of three independent factors as implying they must move together, when the text says each 'can improve independently'

options.text: Effective compute is driven mostly by chip production, with hardware and software efficiency contributing smaller, secondary gains.
options.provenance: misreads the car analogy (cars/speed/driving efficiency) as ranking the three factors by importance rather than establishing them as equal, multiplied terms

explanation: Effective compute is a product of three multiplicative, independently-improving terms — chip count, hardware efficiency per chip, and software efficiency — not a restatement of chip count in different units. Your colleague's framing is exactly the pre-redefinition view this idea sets aside: it treats compute as a hardware-only quantity, missing the software and per-chip efficiency multipliers stacked on top. The 'move together' option gets the multiplication backwards — independence, not lockstep, is the point; one term can hold still while the others keep rising. The 'chip production dominates' option ranks the three the way the car analogy's number-of-cars term might suggest, but all three enter the product as equal partners, not one primary driver with two minor add-ons. (Forecasting Timelines → Effective Compute)
takeaway: Effective compute is chips times hardware efficiency times software efficiency, and 'more compute' claims that only count chips are missing two of the three multipliers.

self_check.cover_test: Yes — a reader who read the Effective Compute discussion can name the three multiplicative factors and their independence without seeing the options.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might default to 'more chips = more compute' as the obviously-true-sounding option, but that's the exact naive view the question is built to catch, not a tell that works.

stem: Suppose chip production growth stalls completely for two years while software and hardware efficiency keep improving at their prior pace. Under the effective-compute framework, what happens to effective compute over those two years?

options.text: It keeps growing, just more slowly than before, because the other two factors keep compounding on their own.
It also stalls, because chip count is the base factor that the other two multiply on top of.
options.provenance: misreads the multiplicative relationship as a dependency chain rather than three equal, independent terms

options.text: It stays flat, because real compute growth is fundamentally about hardware, and software gains don't add genuine compute.
options.provenance: misreads 'compute means more than just counting GPUs' as false, treating compute as a hardware-only quantity

options.text: It shrinks, because a stall in chip production signals falling investment that would soon slow the other two factors as well.
options.provenance: invents a causal coupling between the three factors that the text's independence claim ('each factor can improve independently') explicitly rules out

explanation: Because the three terms multiply independently, a stall in one doesn't zero out the product — it just removes that term's contribution to the growth rate while the other two keep compounding, so effective compute keeps rising, only more slowly. The 'it also stalls' option treats chip count as a dependency the other two sit on top of rather than an equal, independent multiplicand; if that were true, effective compute could never grow faster than raw chip production does on its own. The 'stays flat' option denies that software gains count as compute at all, which is the exact redefinition this idea exists to correct. The 'shrinks' option invents a causal link from a hardware slowdown to falling investment elsewhere that the independence claim specifically rules out. (Forecasting Timelines → Effective Compute)

self_check.cover_test: Yes — a reader who understands the three factors multiply independently can reason through the stalled-chips case unaided.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might guess 'it stalls too' as the intuitive worst-case answer, but that requires not having registered that the factors are independent, which the section states directly.

stem: A commentator writes: 'The Atlas predicts AGI will arrive around 2045.' Which objection is best supported by treating forecasts as consistency checks rather than as concrete predictions?

options.text: 2045 is a rough center of a decades-wide range, not a confident prediction — the range's width, roughly twelve orders of magnitude, is what's informative.
The real problem is that 2045 is being presented as a confident, specific prediction, so the objection should focus on whether that year holds up.
options.provenance: misreads the worked contrast ('somewhere in the 2030s-2050s range, with 2045 as a rough center — not a precise date') as the opposite, treating the center point as the claim under dispute

options.text: The wide error margins around any such estimate show the forecasting approach has failed to produce anything worth acting on.
options.provenance: misreads 'all forecasts come with wide error margins that compound over time' as undermining the method, reversing the point that the margins are themselves the informative output

options.text: The estimate should be dismissed outright, since a method whose range spans that many orders of magnitude has clearly broken down.
options.provenance: misreads the wide biological-anchors bounds (~10^28 to ~10^41 FLOP) as evidence the method failed, rather than as an honestly-reported range that still bounds planning

explanation: The stated figure is a rough center of a range spanning decades, not a specific date to defend or attack — forecasts here work as scenarios for testing whether your beliefs cohere, not as predictions to adopt. The range itself, spanning roughly twelve orders of magnitude of uncertainty in how much compute general intelligence needs, is the thing worth reasoning about. One wrong option treats 2045 as a confident prediction and argues about the year, missing that the center point was never the claim. Another treats wide error margins as proof the exercise failed, reversing the point that a margin's width is itself informative. A third dismisses the estimate because its range is wide, when an honestly wide range still bounds planning better than false precision would. (Forecasting Timelines)
takeaway: A wide forecast range is the finding, not a failure — the width tells you how deep the uncertainty runs, and the midpoint was never the claim.
load_bearing_figures: roughly twelve orders of magnitude of uncertainty in compute-for-TAI estimates (durable, R11 budget candidate for this section)

self_check.cover_test: Yes — a reader who grasps 'forecasts as consistency checks' and the anchor-uncertainty range can articulate this objection without the options.

note: Targets FT-2 and FT-4 together via their discrimination_pairs entry (a claim like 'the chapter predicts 2045' conflates the two): FT-4 supplies the range/width and FT-2 supplies why a center point isn't the claim. A single contrast/objection question does this more cleanly than two separate ones would.

stem: Suppose you combine several individually plausible growth-rate assumptions about investment, software, and hardware, and the combination implies TAI arrives far sooner than you expected. What does treating forecasts as consistency checks, rather than predictions, say you should do with that surprise?

options.text: Treat it as a signal to re-examine one or more of the input assumptions, not as a new prediction to adopt outright.
Adopt the combined result as the best available estimate, since it draws on real trend data.
options.provenance: misreads 'if you're surprised, maybe one of your input beliefs needs updating' as license to trust the combined output instead of as an instruction to re-examine an input

options.text: Conclude that the scaling laws underlying these trends must be mistaken, since they produced an implausible outcome.
options.provenance: conflates a surprising forecast-consistency exercise with the separate empirical claim scaling laws make, misfiling the surprise under the wrong concept

options.text: Set the exercise aside, since a method capable of producing a surprising result isn't a trustworthy way to reason about the future.
options.provenance: misreads 'all forecasts come with wide error margins that compound over time' as undermining the method, when producing a traceable surprise is exactly how the exercise is useful

explanation: Forecasting here works as a consistency check: when combining several individually plausible growth-rate assumptions yields a conclusion that surprises you, that surprise is information about your inputs, not a new fact about the world. The right move is to go back and identify which input rate you were overconfident in. One wrong option treats the surprising combined result as itself the best estimate — exactly the trust-the-output move the exercise warns against. Another blames the scaling laws behind the inputs, filing a forecasting surprise under the wrong concept entirely. A third gives up on the method, when producing a surprising result you can trace back to a shaky assumption is precisely what makes the exercise useful. (Forecasting Timelines)

self_check.cover_test: Yes — a reader who understood forecasts-as-consistency-checks can state the 'update the input' move without seeing the options.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might pick 'adopt the combined result' since it sounds like the exercise's payoff, but that inverts the stated instruction to treat surprise as a prompt to update inputs.

stem: Suppose future research shows that AI-generated synthetic data reliably degrades model quality, closing off that escape route from the data wall, while multimodal data and task-based self-play remain viable. What follows for whether the data wall stops scaling?

options.text: The data wall's fate isn't settled — the other two routes are independent of synthetic data's failure, so it still depends on how well multimodal and self-play data perform.
The data wall stops scaling, because synthetic data was the primary route and the other two were only backups.
options.provenance: misreads the three escape routes as a ranked list with one primary path, when the text presents them as parallel, independent alternatives

options.text: The data wall stops mattering, because multimodal data alone was already described as enough to cover the gap.
options.provenance: misreads the stated 3-10x multimodal expansion estimate as a guaranteed sufficiency rather than a range that leaves the outcome open

options.text: The data wall stops mattering, because task-based self-play can already replace pretraining data for most tasks.
options.provenance: misreads the AlphaZero example as an established general capability rather than a route the text flags as 'still very speculative' and limited to tasks formalizable with explicit rules

explanation: The three data-wall escape routes are independent of each other, so one route failing doesn't settle whether scaling continues — that depends on how the remaining two perform. Treating synthetic data as the 'primary' route with the others as backups isn't how the section frames them; it lists three parallel alternatives, not a ranked list. Treating multimodal data alone as already sufficient overstates what a stated multiplier range guarantees — a 3-10x expansion is a range, not a certainty, and doesn't settle the outcome by itself. And generalizing task-based self-play, which is explicitly flagged as speculative and currently limited to tasks with formalizable rules like Go or Chess, to cover most future tasks overstates how far that route has actually been shown to extend. (Forecasting Timelines → Training Data)
takeaway: The three data-wall escape routes are independent, so one failing tells you nothing about the other two — the honest answer is 'it depends,' not a verdict either way.

self_check.cover_test: Yes — a reader who registers that the three routes are independent alternatives can say 'it depends on the other two' without seeing the options.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might pick whichever option sounds most decisive (stops, or continues fine), but the section deliberately withholds a verdict, which the confident-sounding options both fabricate.

stem: A reader concludes: 'Once we exhaust public text on the internet, AI scaling grinds to a halt.' What does treating the data wall as a soft constraint with multiple escape routes show is wrong with this reasoning?

options.text: The conclusion skips the point that text exhaustion closes off only one input among several viable alternatives.
The conclusion is correct, since the alternative data sources are speculative research directions rather than usable substitutes today.
options.provenance: over-generalizes the 'still very speculative' caveat attached specifically to task-based self-play to all three routes, when synthetic data is described as already working for some domains

options.text: The conclusion has cause and effect backwards — running low on text data would speed up scaling by forcing more efficient algorithms.
options.provenance: invents an accelerating effect from data exhaustion that has no basis in the text's account of the wall

options.text: The conclusion is correct, but for a different reason: effective compute, not data, is really the constraint on scaling.
options.provenance: borrows the true effective-compute idea from earlier in the section and drops it into a question about data, treating two separately-examined constraints as one

explanation: Exhausting public text closes off one input to training, not all of them — the same discussion that names the text wall immediately lists several independent alternatives, so exhaustion alone doesn't determine whether scaling stops. The option calling the alternatives purely speculative overgeneralizes a caveat attached to one route, self-play, to all three; synthetic data is described as already working for some domains today. The 'backwards causality' option invents an accelerating effect exhaustion doesn't have. And the option crediting effective compute instead of data borrows a true idea from elsewhere and drops it into a question it doesn't answer — the data wall and the compute trend are separate constraints, examined separately. (Forecasting Timelines → Training Data)

self_check.cover_test: Yes — a reader who read the three escape routes can name the reader's error (ignoring the alternatives) without seeing the options.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might agree the reader's claim 'sounds right' since running out of data sounds intuitively limiting, but the section explicitly lists working alternatives that block that intuition.

stem: Not knowing how much compute general intelligence requires is compared to not knowing whether something costs one dollar or a trillion dollars — an uncertainty spanning many orders of magnitude. What point does this comparison make about the biological-anchors estimates?

options.text: The comparison shows that the disagreement is about which reference process is even the right one to use, not about a range with a knowable middle.
The comparison shows that the upper and lower bounds are about equally likely, so the true figure is near the middle of the range.
options.provenance: misreads the dollar-or-trillion-dollars analogy as implying a uniform-ish distribution rather than illustrating genuine deep uncertainty about which reference process is right

options.text: The comparison shows that the biological-anchors approach has failed and should be replaced with a method giving a narrower estimate.
options.provenance: misreads the wide bounds (~10^28 to ~10^41 FLOP) as evidence the method failed, rather than as an honestly-reported range that still bounds planning

options.text: The comparison shows that, like prices, compute requirements will converge over time as research settles on a consensus figure.
options.provenance: borrows a market-convergence intuition from the dollar analogy's surface framing that has no counterpart in the text's account of structural, method-level uncertainty

explanation: The comparison is about which underlying reference process for estimating brain-equivalent compute is even the right one to use, not about a symmetric spread around a knowable true value — deep uncertainty of that kind doesn't collapse into 'probably the middle.' The 'equally likely, so probably the middle' option is exactly the reasoning the dollar-or-trillion-dollars analogy exists to block: a range that wide reflects disagreement about method, not a distribution you can average across. The 'method has failed' option mistakes an honestly wide range for a broken estimate, when width is the finding here, not a defect. The 'will converge like prices' option borrows a market intuition with no analogue in this kind of structural uncertainty. (Forecasting Timelines)
takeaway: Twelve orders of magnitude of uncertainty means disagreement about which method is right, not a wide-but-centered guess — there's no honest 'probably the middle.'

self_check.cover_test: Yes — a reader who grasps why the biological-anchors range is so wide can state the 'disagreement about method, not a symmetric spread' point unaided.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might reach for 'probably the middle' as the sensible-sounding default for any wide range, but that is precisely the intuition the analogy is written to defeat.

stem: A reader says: 'If we expect a short AI timeline, that also means we should expect a fast, explosive takeoff.' What is being conflated here?

options.text: Timelines address when transformative AI arrives; takeoff speed — a separate question this section sets aside — addresses how fast capabilities grow once it's close.
Nothing is being conflated — a short timeline and a fast takeoff are just two ways of describing the same underlying risk.
options.provenance: misreads 'predicting when AI automates cognitive labor' (a timelines question) as equivalent to the takeoff-speed question this section does not address

options.text: The framing has it backwards: takeoff speed is what determines when transformative AI arrives, and timelines describe what happens afterward.
options.provenance: reverses which concept answers 'when' and which answers 'what happens after,' swapping the two definitions this section and Takeoff draw apart

options.text: The distinction barely matters in practice, since timeline forecasts are mostly of academic interest and don't change which safety approach is worth pursuing now.
options.provenance: misreads the opening contrast (soon-arriving TAI needs fast, current-system-compatible approaches; distant TAI leaves room for theoretical work) as background motivation rather than a claim that timeline length is itself strategy-determining

explanation: Timelines and takeoff speed answer different questions: timelines are about when transformative AI arrives, and takeoff speed — a question this section sets aside — is about how fast capabilities grow once it's close. A short timeline is compatible with either a gradual or an explosive transition once TAI is near. The 'nothing is being conflated' option collapses that distinction entirely. The 'backwards' option swaps which concept answers 'when' and which answers 'what happens after.' The 'barely matters' option gets it backwards in a different way: timeline length is presented as what determines which safety strategies are even viable, from fast current-system-compatible fixes to slower theoretical research — the opposite of an academic detail with no bearing on strategy. (Forecasting Timelines)
takeaway: A short timeline says nothing on its own about whether the transition is gradual or explosive — that's a separate question the section deliberately leaves open.

self_check.cover_test: Yes — a reader who separates 'when' from 'how fast' can name the conflation without seeing the options.
self_check.cynic_test: A skipper might treat 'short timeline' and 'fast takeoff' as synonyms because both sound urgent, but the section explicitly reserves takeoff speed for a different discussion, which the key names directly.
